newsitem.title: JAPAN: SOCCER-LATE JAPANESE PENALTY DENIES SOUTH KOREA VICTORY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-LATE JAPANESE PENALTY DENIES SOUTH KOREA VICTORY.

text.p: Japan and South Korea took their strained co-hosting of the 2002 World Cup to extreme limits here on Wednesday when they drew 1-1 in a match to celebrate winning the right to stage the tournament.

The draw kept intact South Korea's 25-year-old record of never losing to Japan in Japan and possibly saved -- for the moment -- Japanese coach Shu Kamo's job as his side heads into crucial qualifying games for next year's World Cup in France.
In a match that drew a capacity crowd of nearly 60,000 and proved that soccer in Japan can still come alive for the right game, both sides gave no quarter.
Two Japanese players were shown yellow cards and South Korea had to be content with a draw when a penalty with just two minutes left allowed Japan to save their honour.

Japan attacked throughout the first half which ended goalless but it was a different story in the second half as South Korea, with the wind behind them at Tokyo's National Stadium, went on the attack.
In the 56th minute, defender Sang Chul-yoo scored with a 20-metre header from a corner that delighted hundreds of South Koreans who travelled to Tokyo for the match.
But with the match in South Korea's grasp, Japan were awarded a penalty two minutes from time.
Japan's star player Kazuyoshi Miura struck home the equaliser with ease, silencing South Korean fans and setting off a drumbeat of celebration among the Japanese.
"It was really a tough game. But although time was running out, I always thought we had a chance," Miura said.
There was little work for security guards drafted in to keep peace between fans whose passions run as high as in an England-Germany or Brazil-Argentina game.
The two teams' rivalry is rooted in Japan's colonialisation of Korea at the turn of this century and its actions there during World War Two.
When Japan beat South Korea in a 1993 World Cup qualifier a headline in a Seoul newspaper at the time read:"A national shame unmatched since the annexation by Japan".
Accusations of skullduggery flew in Japan and South Korea's campaign to win the right to stage the 2002 World Cup.
Soccer's world governing body FIFA was reduced to passing a Solomon-like judgement, announcing the tournament would be co-hostied for the first time.

Since then, the World Cup has been on the agenda of every meeting between Japanese and South Korean political leaders, with each assuring the other there would be no attempt to get an advantage in staging the cup.
"Although it was a draw, I'm just relieved it was a good game," a Japanese soccer official said.

Japanese coach Kamo, whose job is under threat because of recent poor performances by the national team, including their failure to reach the final round of last year's Asian Cup, said with more aggression he believes his team could have won.
"But Japan-South Korea games are always special and everyone ends up playing cautiously," he said.
In matches between the two teams since they first clashed in 1954, Korea has now won 32, Japan nine with 14 drawn.
